A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DQO research despite the changed title. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and the retained methods, proofs, experiments, figures and tables can be matched across the reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original DQO experiments on GSM8K, CNN/DailyMail, Dolly and CommonGen, including quality/diversity comparisons, hyperparameter ablations and GPT-4o-mini evaluations.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark results and adds city-recommendation experiments, component ablations, runtime measurements and human diversity evaluations.

M1.justification: The core reward-plus-log-determinant objective, identity regularization and leave-one-out estimator remain. v3 additionally implements Gaussian-kernel and variable identity-weight variants in Appendix D.2, extending the tested procedure beyond v1's dot-product kernel and fixed identity weight without replacing default DQO.

E1.justification: The four original benchmark task families remain. v3 adds a controlled city-recommendation task and a small synthetic simulation with imbalanced three-dimensional embeddings. These are bounded additions to coverage; the human study reuses the existing benchmarks.

E2.justification: v1's benchmark comparisons use reward-only PPO/GRPO. v3 Table 1 additionally evaluates GRPO-likelihood and GRPO-entropy on Dolly and GSM8K, substantially strengthening the comparator set. The city experiment also compares determinant-based DQO against a pairwise-distance variant, and the synthetic simulation introduces uniform sampling as a comparator.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, base models and training configurations are retained. New evaluation designs include 100 city generations at temperature 1.0, an 18-prompt human study with four responses per model and randomized model order, component-setting sweeps, and seconds-per-optimization-step measurements. These introduce substantive protocols beyond the original benchmark evaluation.

E4.justification: v3 adds determinant-versus-pairwise mechanism testing, embedding-model and kernel ablations, identity-weight sensitivity, computational-cost analysis, human validation of the LLM judge, and concrete reward-hacking examples. The original alpha/k ablations and temperature/training-step Pareto analyses were already present and are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. Averaging two order-swapped GPT-4o-mini comparisons is already documented in v1 Appendix E and retained in v3 Appendix I. The new human and timing tables provide point estimates without additional uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial comparator, component, city-frequency, timing and human-evaluation results. Existing GSM8K pass@1 entries also change: v1 Table 3 reports GRPO 73.6 and DQO 74.7 at alpha=1, k=4; v3 Table 6 reports 76.8 and 76.3, reversing their ordering while retaining pass@10 values of 87.9 and 91.2. These revisions are unexplained. The original Dolly hyperparameter table remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The original DPP definitions, reward-augmented embedding proof and eigenvalue bounds are retained. v3 adds a D-optimal-design derivation in Section 3.2 and a weighted log-determinant optimization formulation in Appendix B. This is a limited theoretical extension; its asserted equality det(ZZ^T)=det(Z^TZ) is invalid for general rectangular Z.

C1.justification: Both versions principally claim that DPP-based post-training improves semantic diversity while maintaining response quality across the same four task families. The new contribution bullets largely restate these claims. PPO/GRPO compatibility is highlighted more explicitly but was already demonstrated in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning rare-direction coverage, embedding/kernel robustness, human–LLM judgment agreement and computational overhead. Appendix D explains how reducing identity regularization prioritizes diversity and how alpha moderates the resulting quality loss. The original outcome-reward hacking and embedding-dependence limitations remain, with their discussion reorganized and applicability boundaries stated more explicitly.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access link, baseline regularization coefficients, alternative encoder identities, kernel and identity-weight specifications, timing measurements, and the city prompt. It also newly explains training-reward normalization and pass@n as the highest reward among sampled responses. These improve documentation; they do not establish changes to the retained experiments' underlying settings.

R1.justification: The original lexical-versus-semantic diversity positioning remains. v3 adds connections to D-optimal design and semantic representations, acknowledges concurrent work by Tuyls et al., and cites He et al. for the new likelihood baseline. It also adds supporting RL/metric references and removes Go et al.; moving related work to Appendix A is structural.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work moves to Appendix A, RL background becomes a separate preliminary subsection, quality/diversity/Pareto discussions are consolidated, and detailed reward-hacking discussion moves into Appendix G. The introduction is rewritten with explicit contributions, the experiments gain guiding questions, and the title and conclusion are revised.

P2.justification: v3 adds an opening summary chart, a method diagram, a city-frequency visualization and numerous comparison/analysis tables. The retained quality and radar plots change from two-by-two grids to compact four-panel rows, while the Pareto plots remain. Conference formatting, table placement and appendix layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: The new diversity-aware baselines, component tests and human evaluation strengthen evidence previously centered on reward-only comparisons, while code-access and implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. However, the gains are tempered by inconsistent repeated-setting scores, such as Dolly pass@1 of 5.92 in Tables 1–2 versus 6.56 in Tables 7–8, and the invalid rectangular-matrix determinant identity added in Section 3.2. The paper offers better empirical scrutiny, but these issues limit the net improvement.
